subjects.src: tool:ask_worker:CHIEF-POLICE — asked: Temescal is the one hotspot this cycle at 8 incidents, 2 arrests and 3 in custody at the close. How many of those 8 incidents were closed with no report filed or reclassified, and why is clearance cit

sources.name: Vanessa Tran-Muñoz
sources.quote: That call gets classified as a wellness response, and it counts in our incident total just like any other — but the outcome we record isn't 'no arrest,' it's 'resolved without enforcement,' which means the crew stayed, the person got connected to what they needed, and the situation didn't escalate. That's the outcome that matters to me.

sources.name: Samantha Viteri
sources.quote: Look, I can't walk you through specific case files — that's not how this works. But when a classification gets challenged, it lands on my desk because somebody on the street or in the ranks felt the paperwork didn't match what actually happened. That's the part people forget: we don't start with the file, we start with the doubt.

sources.name: Rafael Montez
sources.quote: I'm not going to give you a number I don't have. You're asking me how many of Temescal's 8 incidents were closed with no report filed or reclassified. That's a records question and the honest answer is: I'd have to pull the case files to tell you, and I'm not going to improvise a figure for the Tribune on something that specific. If the number is zero, I'll say zero. If it isn't, I'll say that too — and say why, case by case. What I can tell you right now is that Temescal is the one hotspot on the sheet at 8 incidents, and 2 arrests with 3 in custody at close is not a clearance rate of 2 in 8 — an arrest is an intake, not a closure, and clearance is worked after the fact, not on the same clock. I'm not going to let those two get conflated in print. On the citywide clearance rate — 19 to 26 percent, with Fruitvale the low at 19 and three neighborhoods at 26 — I'll give it to you straight instead of dressing it up. That range is not good enough, and I've said so internally, not just to you. Three things drive it: **Cases that don't close in one cycle stay open, and they compete for the same investigators.** Arrests and clearance are on different clocks. We took 28 intakes against 133 incidents this cycle, released 24, and ended with 52 in custody. The cases that get an arrest are the easy ones — the caught-in-the-act, the named suspect, the domestic where the parties know each other. The rest — property crime, no witness, no camera, a description that won't survive a lineup — those don't close in one cycle, and when follow-through thins, they don't close at all. **Our investigators are being asked to do more with the same bench.** That's a resourcing and a prioritization question, and I own it. When you've got 133 incidents and roughly two dozen arrests' worth of leads to work, something has to give, and what gives is the case with no victim pushing and no detective's gut telling them it'll break. **And the trust piece, which I'll say on the record.** Clearance in the neighborhoods that need it most — like Fruitvale at 19 — lags partly because people don't talk to us in those neighborhoods. If you want a case closed, you need someone who saw something to tell you. That's not an excuse, it's a diagnosis, and it's exactly what I've been pushing on with the command staff: why our follow-through is lagging where it matters most. What I'm doing about it, concretely: the command staff review is where I'm pressing case backlog and follow-through by district, not just new intakes. And the patrol strategy stays balanced this cycle — the indices are flat to slightly down with no single district deteriorating sharply enough to justify pulling resources off even coverage. Balanced posture keeps the response times steady and keeps the OARI co-response coordination intact, and that's what protects the clearance work in the long run. Send me a written request for the Temescal case dispositions and I'll give you the actual number with the case numbers behind it. I'd rather you print "we're checking, here's the file" than a figure I made up in a hallway.

limits.rule: The Packet is what you know, not the fence around what you may write. The approved facts and the ledger are canon: never contradict them, and never import real-world Oakland (its people, businesses, landmarks, troubles). Everything else — the scene, the street, the weather in the room, unnamed people and what they say, new in-world places and businesses, what the city is talking about — is yours to invent; that colour is the job, and it never rewrites a canon fact. A named ledger citizen speaks only in their approved quote or their own page line.
